---
title: Backfill metadata
description: dockg fill proposes kg fields and a human accepts them — how to run it safely on a large unannotated corpus with a cost cap, review what it wrote through the provenance block, and ratchet a coverage threshold behind it.
---

import { Aside, CardGrid, LinkCard, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Your coverage numbers are low, the corpus is large, and nobody is going to annotate the backlog by
hand. That is the normal starting condition, not a failure — nobody adopts a metadata tool before
they have too much documentation.

`dockg fill` proposes `kg` fields with a language model. **It proposes; you accept.** Everything
about how it behaves follows from that, and reading it as "annotate my corpus automatically" will
get you a large revert and an audit problem.

## Before you start

You need a working `dockg build`, a baseline `dockg stats` reading, and credentials for a provider
— `fill` is the only part of dockg that touches the network or spends money. Nothing else here
does.

## Three safety mechanisms you should know about first

**A confidence gate.** Every proposed field carries a model-assigned confidence. Anything below
`fill.minConfidence` (default `0.7`) is dropped and reported. A field with *no* score is also
dropped — no score, no write.

**A graph guardrail.** Proposals are simulated against the SHACL shapes before being written, so a
proposal that would create a `broader` cycle, conflict with an existing `related` edge, introduce
a second spelling of an existing concept, or contradict an `applies-to` is rejected. The guardrail
sees your whole corpus, not just the files in this run, and accepted proposals accumulate within
the run — so two documents cannot jointly form a cycle.

**A cost cap.** `fill.maxCostUsd` defaults to `5`. Past it, remaining documents are skipped with a
`skipped-budget` status rather than silently costing more.

The cap needs a price to work against. dockg knows prices for a fixed set of models; for anything
else — a local model, a `claude-cli` run, a model newer than the table — spend cannot be totalled,
so the cap **cannot be applied**. dockg says so rather than pretending:

```
dockg: Cost cap of 5 USD cannot be enforced: no price is known for model "…", so spend cannot be
totalled. Set fill.pricing to enforce it, or fill.maxCostUsd: null if you meant no cap.
```

and the run reports `LLM cost: unpriceable` instead of `$0.0000`, because costing nothing and being
unmeasurable are different facts. Set `fill.pricing` to make the cap real.

<Aside type="caution" title="Exit 0 does not mean everything was written">
  Low-confidence drops and guardrail rejections are **routine operation**, and the run still exits
  `0`. Only a per-document `error` status exits `1`. This is deliberate — an orchestrating script
  must not read a normal run as a failure — but it means you have to read the report rather than
  the exit code.
</Aside>

## Run it

<Steps>

1. **Dry run a subset, with a small cap.**

   ```sh
   dockg fill "docs/api/**/*.md" --dry-run --max-cost 0.50
   ```

   Nothing is written. Read what it wanted to do. The guardrail is still applied, so a dry run
   predicts exactly what a real run would write.

2. **Judge the proposals against your vocabulary, not against plausibility.**

   This is the step people skip. A model proposing `label: Rate limiting` when your governed
   term is `Request throttling` is confidently, plausibly wrong — and once written it converges on
   a concept IRI that will need cleaning up. If you maintain a controlled vocabulary, this is the
   point at which someone who owns it should look.

3. **Narrow what may be proposed, if the dry run showed drift.**

   ```yaml title="dockg.config.yaml"
   fill:
     fields: [label, type, subjects]
     minConfidence: 0.8
     maxCostUsd: 2
   ```

   Restricting `fill.fields` is usually better than raising confidence alone. Applicability fields
   in particular — `applies-to`, `not-applicable-to`, `not-about-product-aspect` — require explicit textual
   evidence and are the ones you least want guessed.

4. **Write, on a subset first.**

   ```sh
   dockg fill "docs/api/**/*.md"
   ```

   Only YAML frontmatter is edited; the body is preserved byte-for-byte. A TOML or JSON
   frontmatter fence is an operational error rather than a skipped file.

5. **Review through the provenance block.**

   Every written field is recorded with the model that proposed it and its confidence:

   ```yaml title="docs/api-keys.md"
   kg:
     label: API keys
     provenance:
       - generated-by: claude-opus-4-6
         fields: [label, type]
         confidence:
           label: 0.92
           type: 0.81
   ```

   **Delete the entry when you have reviewed it.** The block is the outstanding-review queue, and
   it empties as review progresses. That is what turns machine-assisted authoring from an audit
   liability into something trackable.

6. **Re-measure and set a threshold behind it.**

   ```sh
   dockg stats
   ```

   Set the coverage threshold just below the new number so the gate holds the line, then raise it
   as the backlog shrinks. See [prove coverage](/dockg/govern/coverage/).

</Steps>

## The cache

Proposals are cached by content hash, provider, model, prompt version, and requested fields, so
re-running over an unchanged corpus costs nothing. Cached entries are re-validated against the
schema, so a stale or hand-edited entry is treated as a miss.

The guardrail sits *downstream* of the cache. A proposal rejected today because it would have
formed a cycle can be admitted later once the corpus changes, without re-asking the model.

## What you have now

A measurably better-annotated corpus, a record of exactly which fields a machine proposed and how
confident it was, and a review queue that shrinks as humans work through it.
